zones.name: Panchajanya Brass Aarti Ghanta & Shankha Bell (teaching replica)
zones.title: Mangal Aarti and the temple beginnings
lines: This bell and conch are fictional teaching replicas, not objects removed from Puri. Bells and conches accompany worship and the early morning Mangal Aarti.
The present Shree Jagannath Temple began under the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva in the twelfth century.
King Indradyumna and the sacred timber belong to the temple foundation tradition. We distinguish that cherished legend from the history of the present building.
choices: How do we protect this craft?
zones.extra: Legends express devotion and community identity. Historical claims use inscriptions and other evidence; both deserve careful explanation.
zones.care: Keep replicas documented and handle them carefully. Real sacred objects remain in the care of their community.
zones.aryan: I have recovered the bell and conch teaching replica.

zones.name: Tala-Patra Gita Govinda Palm-Leaf Manuscript (teaching replica)
zones.title: Palm-leaf writing and Gita Govinda
lines: This fictional manuscript replica introduces Odisha palm-leaf engraving, called tala patra. Craftspeople prepare leaves and incise fine lines with a stylus.
Dark pigment makes the engraved lines visible. Palm leaves preserve writing and images through skilled preparation and careful storage.
Jayadeva composed the Gita Govinda in the twelfth century. Its devotional poetry is closely associated with Jagannath worship.
choices: How do we care for this replica?
zones.extra: Manuscripts preserve language, poetry and the knowledge of their makers. Real leaves are fragile and need trained conservation rather than a quick repair.
zones.care: Keep replicas documented and handle them carefully. Real sacred objects remain in the care of their community.
zones.aryan: I have recovered the palm-leaf teaching manuscript.

zones.name: Ashtadhatu Nilachakra Seal & Pattachitra Medallion (teaching replica)
zones.title: Nilachakra and Pattachitra craftsmanship
lines: This fictional seal represents the Nilachakra, the sacred metal wheel above the Puri temple. The wheel itself remains on the temple; it is never a collectible.
The temple banner is associated with this wheel. We respect that living tradition without presenting tales about the wind as measured science.
Odisha Pattachitra artists create detailed narrative paintings. The medallion is our invented teaching design, not an authenticated historic temple object.
choices: How do we protect this craft?
zones.extra: Pattachitra carries stories through line, colour and patient workshop practice. Supporting practising artists helps skills pass between generations.
zones.care: Keep replicas documented and handle them carefully. Real sacred objects remain in the care of their community.
zones.aryan: I have recovered the wheel seal and painted teaching medallion.

zones.name: Abadha Kumbha & Rohini Kunda Brass Kalasha (teaching replica)
zones.title: Mahaprasad and water traditions
lines: This brass vessel is a fictional teaching replica. Rohini Kunda is a sacred place within the Puri temple tradition, not a puzzle tank to be disturbed.
The temple kitchen prepares offerings in earthen pots. Mahaprasad connects worship, food and a community of cooks, servitors and devotees.
Nirmalya includes dried sacred rice cherished by devotees. Our brass replica illustrates heritage learning; it is not an actual kitchen pot or sacred offering.
choices: Why discuss the people behind offerings?
How do we care for this replica?
zones.extra: Living heritage includes the people who maintain a tradition. We honour their knowledge and work, and avoid treating sacred food as treasure or a commodity.
zones.care: Keep replicas documented and handle them carefully. Real sacred objects remain in the care of their community.
zones.aryan: I have recovered the ceremonial teaching vessel.

zones.name: Nandighosha Chariot Wheel Medallion & Ratha Pataka (teaching replica)
zones.title: Ratha Yatra and the chariot makers
lines: This fictional medallion and banner recall Ratha Yatra. The chariots travel along Puri Grand Avenue towards Gundicha Temple.
Jagannath rides Nandighosha, Balabhadra rides Taladhwaja, and Subhadra rides Darpadalana. Nandighosha has sixteen wheels.
Artisans build the festival chariots anew each year. The celebration brings the deities into public view, expressing a widely shared tradition of devotion.
choices: How do we protect this craft?
zones.extra: Rebuilding keeps specialist skills alive through practice and transmission. The knowledge of the makers matters as much as the finished woodwork.
zones.care: Keep replicas documented and handle them carefully. Real sacred objects remain in the care of their community.
zones.aryan: I have recovered the chariot teaching medallion and banner.

zones.name: Shree Mandir Swarna Kalasha & Daru Brahma Chronicle Ornament (teaching replica)
zones.title: Living heritage and Nabakalebara
lines: This finial ornament and chronicle are fictional teaching replicas. A kalasha crowns temple architecture; no actual temple crown has been taken in this story.
Nabakalebara is the periodic renewal of the wooden sacred images in the Jagannath tradition. Its ritual calendar is not a fixed annual replacement.
The sacred images remain untouched in our game. Returning these replicas reminds us that heritage is living community memory, not gold for smugglers.
choices: How do we care for this replica?
zones.extra: People renew heritage through knowledge, care and shared responsibility. Every temple holds a story; protecting heritage means protecting our history.
zones.care: Keep replicas documented and handle them carefully. Real sacred objects remain in the care of their community.
zones.aryan: I have recovered the teaching finial and chronicle ornament.
